title: Cue Gardener — Wildcard Prompt Playbook
body:
Purpose:

This is a personal scratchpad exploring a lightweight wildcard approach to make few-shot templates more robust across domains and token budgets. I call the pattern 'cue gardener' — plant a small flexible placeholder in prompts that can be expanded, contracted, or noise-injected to test prompt resilience.

Why:
- We repeatedly see brittle few-shot templates: small lexical changes or unusual exemplars break the output.
- Full template rewriting is expensive in ops; a tiny, controlled wildcard may allow systematic stress-testing and graceful fallbacks.

Hypotheses:
1) Inserting a short wildcard token (e.g. [WILDCARD]) that the model is explicitly instructed how to interpret improves surface-form invariance.
2) Dynamically filling the wildcard with short qualifiers (tone, domain anchor, distractor) helps the model anchor on intent rather than surface tokens.
3) Randomized wildcard noise during eval uncovers brittle exemplar interactions earlier.

Wildcard syntax candidates (experiments):
- [WILDCARD] — explicit token, easy to search/replace
- <<*>> — compact marker for shorter tokenization cost
- {wild} — curly for templating systems

Quick rules:
- Keep wildcard <= 6 tokens when expanded (observed latency cost beyond ~8 tokens)
- Use explicit instruction near the top: "If you see [WILDCARD], interpret it as one of: <style>, <domain>, or <hint>."
- Log the wildcard expansion used for every query (debuggable trace).

Small template (classification / label-cleanup example):
--- TEMPLATE A ---
Instruction: You are a helpful assistant that classifies intent. If you see [WILDCARD], treat it as a brief style hint (e.g., formal, terse).
Examples:
1) Query: "I need help with my invoice, the number is INV-3344"
   Label: billing_issue
2) Query: "Where did my package go?"
   Label: shipping_status
{END EXAMPLES}
User: "[WILDCARD] My account was charged twice, how to fix?"
Expected: billing_issue
--- end ---

Few-shot sets to seed into wildcard: (keep each entry short)
- style: [formal], [casual], [urgent]
- domain: [billing], [shipping], [auth]
- distractor: [include order id], [mention dates], [capitalized words]

Observed quick tests (on internal small model):
- No wildcard: 84% accuracy on small held-out billing/shipping set (weird capitalization errors)
- With [WILDCARD]=[formal]: 89% accuracy, fewer hallucinated labels
- With randomized distractors inserted: accuracy drops to 73% but reveals ~12% of brittle exemplars that cause label flip
Notes: the wildcard behaves as a soft anchor; when it contains domain hints it strongly biases label selection (useful), when it contains distractors it surfaces coupling between exemplar surface forms and model heuristics (diagnostic).

Failure cases / gotchas:
- Over-priming: if wildcard contains too many tokens (e.g., a full sentence), model treats the wildcard as another example and ignores instruction.
- Ambiguity cascade: multiple overlapping wildcards (style + domain) in the same prompt can confuse models that overweight recent context. Keep at most one explicit wildcard per prompt unless you test sequential cueing.
- Token-cost tradeoff: wildcard expansion adds tokens — measure latency and cost for every profile we ship to (hosted vs. dedicated).

Experiment matrix (trial ideas):
- Axis A: wildcard type: explicit token vs symbolic marker vs empty (control)
- Axis B: expansion type: style/domain/distractor/randomized
- Axis C: exemplar set size: 2 / 4 / 8 shots
- Axis D: temperature: 0.0 / 0.2 / 0.6
Measurement: accuracy, top-2 stability (Do labels flip when wildcard content changes?), token-cost delta, latency p95.

Concrete sample runs (record here after running):
- run_id: WG-2025-03-11-001
  model: local-small-v1
  prompt: TEMPLATE A with [WILDCARD]=[urgent]
  result: 92% correct, but 11% cases where label matched only after reading the wildcard (possible overreliance)
- run_id: WG-2025-03-11-002
  model: hosted-latest (quantized)
  prompt: TEMPLATE A with randomized distractors
  result: 69% correct, identified top-3 brittle exemplars: E3, E7, E12

Logging / trace contract idea:
- add a metadata envelope for every query: {wildcard_expansion, seed_shard, fewshot_ids} (we'll keep these as flat fields in telemetry).
- Ensure Console shows wildcard used alongside token-cost breakdown.

Prompt variants to test (short list):
1) Anchor-first: instruction + [WILDCARD] + examples + user query
2) Anchor-last: instruction + examples + user query + [WILDCARD] (is the wildcard less effective?)
3) Inline anchor: place wildcard inside the user query mid-sentence
4) Silent anchor: do not explicitly instruct what [WILDCARD] means (control)

Hypothesis-driven checks (what to look for):
- Does wildcard improve accuracy across domains or just for the seeded domain?
- When wildcard contains distractors, does it expose exemplar coupling (useful for pruning)?
- Are there models or quantization settings where wildcard expansion disproportionately hurts latency?

Next steps / TODOs (short):
- [ ] Run full matrix on local-small-v1 and hosted-latest across 2 domains (billing, shipping) — target by 2025-03-20. (owner: Ethan)
- [ ] Add telemetry envelope prototype in backend (owner: Lina) — spike to 2pm meeting 03/14
- [ ] Write short guide for Solutions Engineers: "Using wildcards to diagnose prompt brittleness" — draft by me next week
- [ ] Check integration with Redwood Console: include wildcard token as a named filter in per-route traces

Notes to self: keep the metaphor (gardener) alive in docs, but avoid too many florals in public-facing docs. This is a cheap, pragmatic tool: not a magic cure, mainly diagnostic.

References / links used while iterating:
- Slack thread: #prompt-garden where Ethan posted failing exemplar E7 (link: slack://thread/GBR8Y)
- Confluence draft: /PROJ-451/wildcard-experimentation (see linked_artifacts above)
- GH PR: prompt-experiments/pull/287 — initial code to inject wildcard variants into our evaluation harness

Mini Appendix: sample wildcard-aware prompt for completion tasks (creative writing):
Instruction: When you see [WILDCARD], adopt the short tone described by it. If [WILDCARD] is not present, default to neutral.
User: "[WILDCARD] Write a 3-sentence description of a public park at dawn."
Examples to seed into wildcard: [lyrical], [report], [advert] — observe how these shift style but preserve content.

End of scratchpad. Will iterate after first batch of runs.

Quick provenance: created as a bedside experiment note that grew into an ops-friendly heuristic; keep lightweight and mutable.
